subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Uranus: The Sideways Planet
description: A 60-second lesson on Uranus: The Sideways Planet.

hook.text: Uranus spins on its side, tilted 98 degrees. Each pole faces the Sun for 42 years, then darkness for 42.

buildup.text: It's an ice giant—mostly water, methane, and ammonia ices around a small rocky core.

discovery.text: Methane absorbs red light, giving Uranus its pale blue-green color. It's a frigid −224°C.

twist.text: Something enormous hit Uranus long ago, knocking it sideways. Likely an Earth-sized impactor.

climax.text: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit Uranus, flying past in 1986. It remains barely explored.

punchline.text: Knocked sideways by a cosmic impact. Still spinning alone.

quiz.question: Why does Uranus spin on its side?
options: A massive collision with an Earth-sized object tilted it long ago
The gravity of Neptune gradually pulled it sideways
It formed that way from the original solar nebula

details.summary: Uranus rotates on its side with an axial tilt of 98 degrees — essentially rolling around the Sun rather than spinning upright. This ice giant has a blue-green methane atmosphere, 27 known moons, faint rings, and extreme seasonal cycles where each pole faces the Sun for 42 years at a time.
details.whyItMatters: Uranus's extreme tilt suggests a violent collision early in solar system history. As an ice giant, it represents a poorly understood planetary class — distinct from gas giants and rocky planets — that may be common around other stars.
takeaways: Uranus rotates nearly on its side with a 98-degree axial tilt
Its methane atmosphere gives it a distinctive blue-green color
Each pole experiences 42 years of continuous sunlight or darkness

faq.question: Why is Uranus tilted on its side?
faq.answer: The leading theory is that an Earth-sized protoplanet struck Uranus early in solar system formation, knocking it over. Some models suggest multiple smaller impacts could produce the same effect.

faq.question: Will we send another mission to Uranus?
faq.answer: The 2023 Planetary Science Decadal Survey ranked a Uranus Orbiter and Probe as the highest-priority flagship mission. Only Voyager 2 has visited (1986 flyby).
